The Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan) is a parallel primitive that maps an input list of values to an output list where each element at index $i$ is the sum of all input elements at indices strictly less than $i$ [S2].

The claim states that the Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan) maps an input list to an output list where each element at index $i$ is the sum of all input elements at indices strictly less than $i$. Source [S2] explicitly defines the scan kernel as mapping the input list one-to-one to an output list in parallel, where 'The value of the output list at position 𝑖, is defined to be the sum of all elements of the input list less than 𝑖 (exclusive scan).' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
- **Strengths:** Enables parallel compaction of sparse data structures (e.g., voxels) without race conditions [S2].

The evidence explicitly states that the parallel prefix sum scan kernel allows culled voxels to be 'eliminated from the voxel list independently and in parallel.' This directly supports the claim that the method enables parallel compaction of sparse data structures (voxels) without race conditions, as the exclusive scan provides unique, conflict-free indices for each kept element.
supported
It differs from inclusive scans by excluding the current element from the sum, and from standard sequential scans by providing a parallel algorithmic structure suitable for GPU execution [S1, S2].

The claim states that the method differs from inclusive scans by excluding the current element from the sum. Source [S1] defines the Exclusive Sum S_i as the sum of D_j for j from 0 to i-1, which explicitly excludes the element at index i (D_i). Source [S2] confirms this by stating the output at position i is the sum of all elements less than i. The claim also states it differs from standard sequential scans by providing a parallel algorithmic structure suitable for GPU execution. Source [S1] mentions 'fast parallel methods for EXCLUSIVESUM are available' and treats the problem as 'parallel reductions'. Source [S2] explicitly states the scan kernel maps the input list 'in parallel' and references an 'efficient GPU implementation'. Both parts of the claim are directly supported by the provided evidence.

In volume rendering, it is used for voxel compaction, as described in [S2] for sparse voxelization and in [S1] for neural geometric level of detail rendering.

The evidence in both sources explicitly describes the use of parallel prefix sum (exclusive scan) to compute indices for compacting voxel lists. Source [S2] states that the scan provides the location of kept voxels in a sequential list, allowing culled voxels to be eliminated (voxel compaction) in the context of sparse voxelization (subdivision). Source [S1] describes using the exclusive sum to provide conflict-free write indices for parallel threads, which is the mechanism for compacting data (writing occupied voxels to a dense/compact structure) in the context of neural geometric level of detail rendering.
